x: This reference describes how Middle-earth: Shadow of War works inside: the layout of its executable, the engine objects that run the game, how it streams and stores data, the world format, scripting, rendering, effects, audio, animation and physics, and the gameplay systems built on top of them (AI, combat, items, the Nemesis system, quests, user interface and saves). The engine is Monolith Productions' in-house engine; the build paths left in the executable name the project Kraken ( proj\Kraken\code\... ). It builds on Havok 2016.2.0-r1 ( hk2016 2 0 r1 ) for physics, AI navigation, cloth and scripting (HavokScript), Wwise for audio, Bink 2 for video and Scaleform GFx 4.5 for the user interface.
Everything here describes the Steam release, game version 1.21 ( ShadowOfWar.exe , 117,732,784 bytes, linked in August 2018). Addresses will differ on any other build.

- Static analysis of the executable: a full instruction decode of every function, cross references, vtables and run-time type information, string references, the exception-unwind tables and the C runtime's initializer tables. - Inspection of the running game: reading live objects, containers and engine state, with a control for every census (a known-good object or a deliberately wrong value checked in the same pass), and comparing values decoded from the shipped files with the values the engine holds. - Parsing the shipped archives: every container format and data format the game reads, decoded until every byte of a format is accounted for and the decode matches what the running game loaded. - Thread sampling: suspending one thread at a time, unwinding its stack with the executable's own unwind data, and aggregating thousands of samples into call trees and per-frame order. - Emulation: running individual engine functions in an emulator against a snapshot of live memory, to see exactly what they read and decide. Numbers such as "950 of 950" are the measurements a statement rests on: how many cases were checked and how many agreed.

- The executable has no relocation table, so it always loads at 0x140000000 . Code and static data addresses are given as offsets from that base (RVAs): 0x1A864C is the address 0x140000000 + 0x1A864C = 0x1401A864C. - [base+0x26FFAA8] means "the pointer stored at RVA 0x26FFAA8". [GM+0x6C68] means "the pointer stored 0x6C68 bytes into the object GM". - Heap addresses change every run and are never given. - vt 0x1F68920 names a class by its vtable's RVA when the class has no recoverable name; vf10 is the vtable's eleventh slot (counting from 0). - GameDB records and categories are written in backticks with their category path, for example Character/Models .
Each chapter ends with the questions that are still open, phrased with what would settle them.

t: The executable: sections, functions, vtables, libraries
x: ShadowOfWar.exe is a 64-bit image of 117,732,784 bytes. It has no relocation table ( IMAGE FILE RELOCS STRIPPED , no DYNAMIC BASE ), so it always loads at 0x140000000 and every code and static address is the same in every run; only heap addresses move. Control Flow Guard is off (load configuration of 148 bytes, no guard flags), so the image carries no compiler-made list of address-taken functions.

The section names do not describe their contents. Executability comes from each section's characteristics, not from its name: Section RVA range Access Contents --- --- --- --- .arch 0x0001000 - 0x1D87C00 read, execute the engine's code (about 30 MB) .sdata 0x1D88000 - 0x1D91400 read, execute more code .xtext 0x1D92000 - 0x25AC000 read read-only data: the vtables , strings, the GameDB schema metadata .idata 0x25AC000 - 0x2AA5000 read, write the writable globals: singletons, managers, static objects, startup tables .pdata 0x2AA5000 - 0x2C85000 read the exception directory: 163,575 unwind entries .bss a 0x2C89000 - 0x729714D read, write, execute 70 MB of code (below) .text 0x7299000 - 0x7299014 read, write 20 bytes, not executable Several further small sections hold the import and export directories, resources and other data. .bss a holds engine methods that are reached only through vtables: of 2,134 vtables with recovered starts, 1,847 have at least one method there, and 12,832 of 71,422 vtable slots point into it. None of those methods is the target of a direct call (0 of 400 sampled; the static call graph has 4,371 call sources in the section and no call targets), so a function the

The exception directory is not the list of functions: - Leaf functions have no entry. The x64 ABI requires an unwind entry only for a function that needs unwinding; a leaf (no stack frame, no non-volatile registers touched, no calls) may omit it. The engine's StringHash 0x423E70, with more than 2,000 callers, is one of them. - 16.1% of the entries are fragments : 26,293 of 163,575 carry UNW FLAG CHAININFO and end with their parent's entry (8,140 directly after the parent, 11,001 within 64 KB, 7,152 far away as cold blocks; 12,232 functions own fragments). A fragment is entered by a jump, not a call. - Jump tables sit inline in .arch right after their function (the MSVC form lea rB, [ ImageBase]; mov eJ, [rB + rI 4 + T]; add rJ, rB; jmp rJ ), so a linear disassembly turns their bytes into millions of false instructions. Decoding must follow control flow from known starts and never continue past a terminator. - Tails : 4,822 call-free blocks outside every entry that a function jumps to and back from belong to that function. The function list is therefore 243,839 functions : 137,282 with their own unwind entry and the rest leaves found as call targets, callbacks whose address is only

33,354 qword slots in the writable globals are zero in the file and hold code pointers once the game has started (21,343 distinct targets): registration tables that startup code fills with lea rdx, [function] followed by a call to a register function (only 1,044 slots are written by a direct mov ). Across two launches the slots and their targets agreed with a Jaccard index of 0.9997 over 33,347 slots; the few differences are run-time state (a stored return address and a captured call stack), not tables.

The C runtime entry 0x8C3E5C runs initterm e(0x1DA8778, 0x1DA8798) (C initializers) and initterm(0x1D93950, 0x1DA8760) : 10,690 C++ global constructors , in link order. The first global each constructor writes increases along the table in 8,043 of 9,483 steps (84.8%): data is laid out per object file. Code is not: across 18,206 functions, the correlation between a function's address and the address of its private globals is 0.105 (Spearman), the signature of whole-program optimisation reordering code. Only local runs survive (functions bracketed by one source file's strings belong to that file in 451 of 454 cases). 649 of the constructors register developer-console entries. Each is the same 0x7C-byte body: thread-safe initialisation of the console registry, the static object 0x2A58BC0 (vt 0x1EC6488, a critical section and a sorted entry list, guard 0x2A58BB0, built by 0x816CF4), Register(entry) (registry slot 12), then atexit(unregister) . The registry's Execute is 0x15D0338, Find 0x7CBBA4 and Register 0x77F54C.

Vtables are read-only data in .xtext . 1,546 classes carry MSVC run-time type information (a complete-object locator before the vtable). About 4,100 more do not: 5,007 runs of two or more function pointers in .xtext are loaded by a lea and have no type information; for 4,097 of them (81.8%) the constructor pattern holds, the run's address being stored at [object+0] , against 1,399 of 1,746 (80.1%) for vtables with type information. CResourceBundle (0x1E6E678, 18 slots, constructors 0x3DB434 and 0x3DB6EC) is one of the classes without it. Vtables without type information pack back to back with no separator, so a table's end is the next table's start, and a start needs evidence: a code reference, a data pointer or a run-time pointer to it. A string-guessed start inside another table cuts that table short: the NPC class vt 0x1FB3640 has at least 129 slots (its per-frame AI update is slot 119, and slots 121, 122 and 128 are in use). Multiple inheritance shows as tables side by side: an inventory item's primary vtable 0x1FDABF8 has one slot and its secondary vtable, stored at +0x18 , is 0x1FDABD0 with five. The C runtime's initializer table is not a vtable even though it is a long run o

The build uses link-time code generation, and it shows in the calling convention. Values stay in volatile registers across calls to functions the compiler proved do not touch them: computing each function's written registers as a fixed point over the call graph, 61,578 of 133,050 callees preserve at least one volatile general-purpose register, and between 74,179 and 83,251 preserve a given xmm register (0x1C0B634 keeps the screen width in xmm1 across the screen-height accessor). Analysis that assumes every call clobbers rax, rcx, rdx, r8-r11 loses these values. The linker also folds identical functions . Many script bindings share one implementation, so a function address claimed by many bindings is not an identity: the engine assert 0x819104 (3,226 call sites), the 5-byte operator delete thunk 0x8C4370 (4,839 callers) and the record-name getter 0x18BDB0 (2,203) each sit under many binding names. Binding stubs are packed back to back with no padding (a ret at 0x1B75A4B, the next stub's mov r11, rsp at 0x1B75A4C).

Identified from library strings and source paths, the namespaces of type information, imports, known constants (CRC32, FNV, SHA, MD5, AES tables) and contiguity (libraries link as contiguous object files; a gap bracketed by one library belongs to it, with 622 of 626 held-out anchors confirmed), 13,886 functions belong to linked libraries : Library Functions --- --- Havok (physics, AI navigation, cloth) 8,090 MSVC standard library 2,793 OpenSSL 1,897 Hydra (the publisher's online-services client) 619 Steamworks 327 HavokScript 61 Bink 45 Wwise 34 zlib 17 Exports. The executable exports 286 named symbols with their full C++ signatures: 263 belong to Wwise (the AK::SoundEngine API and its Query , MemoryMgr , StreamMgr , DynamicSequence , Monitor , MotionEngine , MusicEngine and DynamicDialogue namespaces, and globals such as g pRegistryMgr and g pRTPCMgr ; see Audio and video), the rest are Scaleform's system and matrix functions, two memory pool ids and an assert hook. With the run-time type information they are the binary's only exact symbol names. The online layer also links the Apache Avro C library ( avro record set , src\Core\avFloatType.cpp ). In one running game a single state of the second copy owned 123 segments summing exactly to its 2,695 MB footprint , 78% of the process's heap memory: 1,086,315 chunks, 2,663 MB in use. t: Engine core: managers, globals and key objects
x: The engine reaches its subsystems through a small number of pointers stored in the writable globals (the .idata section, 0x25AC000-0x2AA5000). Each is a single slot written once or twice at start-up and read from hundreds or thousands of functions. Heap objects behind them move every run; the slots do not.

Reads and writes are counted over the whole executable (every instruction that addresses the slot). - The spawn manager [base+0x26FFBE8] is null at the main menu and live once a world is loaded. The player object persists across menus, so its presence proves nothing. A world is in play when the spawn manager exists and holds spawned characters. - Spawn manager layout. +0x190 is the number of characters owned by ambient spawning, not the length of the character array. Entries are 0x40 bytes with the character at +0x20 . The manager is reallocated during travel, so a pointer to it must be re-read on every use; the same holds for character controllers, which are replaced on respawn. - A load starting shows as a new pointer at [CGameClientShell]+0xE50 . - Pause. The simulation pauses while the game window is unfocused: the world time stops and the per-object time steps are 0, while the renderer keeps drawing at full rate. - Loads rebuild state. Some loading screens deserialise GameDB instance data and faction members again, and a region change resets bundles and animation state, so values written into those objects before a load do not survive it.

Anything that allocates engine objects, dispatches to scripts or rebuilds a world object runs on the main thread; the render thread consumes commands the main thread posts (see Threads and the frame). Engine asserts are a write to a null address at 0x819113 with the message in rcx ( EngineAssert 0x819104).

- Which class vt 0x1DA9640 is ( [base+0x26FFB40] ; its only constructor is 0x108BB0, called from 0x1081AC). - What the clock state's remaining fields mean ( +0x08 , and +0x38 .. +0x40 , which hold 1, 100 and 1 on most clocks and 1, -1 and 1 on the unscaled one).

The game runs about 94 threads in the world. 35 belong to the executable, about 33 to the graphics driver, and the rest to the C runtime, the OS, Bink (5), XAudio2 and the input stack. The engine names its threads ( GetThreadDescription returns the name); 28 carry a name. Thread Routine (RVA) Role --- --- --- MainThread starts at 0x73D1310, loop 0xC24DB0 the game frame RenderThread 0x1C8F158 consumes the render command ring, renders, presents FXBackgroundThread 0x116B11C effect work GameAudioMgrThread 0x181F638 the engine's audio manager HavokWorkerThread1-3 0x11AFE58 (shared) Havok task workers EngineAnimationJobThread1-3 0x114CBA8 (shared) animation pose jobs ResourceOpenThread / LoaderThread / ParserThread 0x11AECC8 / 0x11AEE50 / 0x11AEF58 the three resource stages (see Resource streaming) ZLibDecompressTask x2, ZLibDecompressThread 0x11AD438, 0x11AD440 decompression StorageRequestThread 0x11C6DB0 storage requests VideoClipRequestThread 0x11C7488 video clip requests DLCPackageMountingThread 0x11ABCF8 mounting DLC packages PathSystemRegionThread, PathFindingThread 0x114AEF0, 0x11E1EA8 navigation AIThread 0x116A3BC AI background work FireSim 0x1A3D998 fire simulation MotionSystem

An engine thread is an object of a small class with 11 virtual methods: vf0 the destructor, vf1 the shared Start 0x529500, vf8 the thread's name, vf9 its start stub and vf10 its stack size (the AI thread, vt 0x22FF668: "AIThread", 0x1AEA674, 0x10000). Start(this, routine, arg) stores the routine at +0x18 , the argument at +0x20 and the name at +0x28 , creates the OS thread suspended on the stub (handle at +0x08 ), applies priority and affinity settings and resumes it. Every stub is a jump to the trampoline 0x797DD4, which names the OS thread and calls routine(arg) . Every engine thread's stack therefore ends at 0x797DD4.

The main loop is 0xC24DB0. Each iteration either does the frame's work under 0x2D47E0 or waits in 0x3807E8 - 0x380FAC - 0x38105C ( MsgWaitForMultipleObjectsEx ). The wait is for the render thread. 0x38105C takes the render command queue (0x272E8D8; see the render thread below) and calls 0x1CF430 with its state block ( +0x38 ). 0x1CF430 loops while the render thread is behind: while the value at +0x198 is below the value at +0x1A0 , or equal to it and the ring's read cursor +0xD0 is still below +0x188 . Each pass sets +0x1EC , signals the render thread's event ( +0x130 ) and waits on its own event ( +0x128 ) with MsgWaitForMultipleObjectsEx , so window messages are still dispatched while the main thread waits; when the stop byte +0x120 is set it only pumps messages ( PeekMessageW ). The main thread can therefore run ahead of the renderer only as far as the queue allows.

Game objects are updated by a per-object countdown, not by a character loop. 0x2D47E0 passes [base+0x26FF050] to 0x1F68D8, which skips the walk while the object server [base+0x26FF058] reports itself busy, then calls 0x6B31DC on the update manager U = [base+0x26FF050]+0x3E0 (vt 0x22C0050). 0x6B31DC first drains a deferred-delivery buffer at U+0x690 (0x4CA9F8): each entry names a target object ( +0x20 ) and a 16-bit tag ( +0x28 ), and 0x4CAD68 decodes the entry's recorded payload in chunks of up to 512 bytes and hands each chunk to the target's vtable slot 19; the buffer is then reset and time-stamped. Then it calls 0x2FA064 : - 0x2FA064 walks the object sets linked from U+0x18 (node at set+0x18 , next at node+0x08 ; 130 sets in a loaded region). For each set it takes the set's due list set+0xE8 and hands every object on it to 0x2FA10C. - 0x2FA10C subtracts the object's time-domain step [[obj+0x88]+0x14] from its countdown obj+0xD0 . If the countdown is still above zero the object goes back on the list; otherwise it tail-jumps to the object's vf18, its Update (vtable +0x90 ), which is why vf18 appears directly under 0x2FA064 in an unwound stack. - SetNextUpdate 0x59AB3C(object, dela

The engine's own byte count understates the real cost of a single bundle and overstates a burst: Nazgul base (36.0 MB by the engine's count) added 120 MB of committed memory and 120 MB of video memory, while 129 bundles requested at once (622 - 4,337 MB by the engine's count) added only 571 MB of video memory and 665 MB of commit, because they share resources. t: Names: what is a file fact and what is a reader trap
x: - A record's name offset points at its own leaf, relative to 0x30. Read that way, with folders taken from the folder table, every typed entry's content matches its extension: 482,736 of 482,736 entries of 16 typed extensions ( .bndl , .embb , .tex , .mesh , .anix , .bnk ...), and each of the 39 extensions in the install maps to one format (catalogue below). No per-archive naming rule is needed. - The pool is not a list of entries in order. It also holds the folder paths, and it stores each leaf string once: 56,018 records share a leaf string with another record ( string.strdb in 14 language folders), while full paths are unique within each archive (0 duplicates). A reader that takes "the string after the previous name", or resolves offsets against a wrong base (0x18 instead of 0x30), names a neighbouring file: on the same records those rules give a name whose extension contradicts the content for 396,483 and 388,454 records. The result looks plausible because a neighbour's name is still a real path. - A path names a file only within one archive; the same path in another archive is another copy, chosen by the search order above.

File data is a chain of chunks, each {u32 stored length, u32 length, bytes} , with every chunk header 4-byte aligned relative to the start of the entry and a record's stored size equal to the chain's length rounded up to 4 (19,993 of 19,993 sampled entries, up to 400 per archive). The chunk reader 0x11DC664: 1. reads the two lengths and asserts "Encountered a corrupted compressed chunk header." when either exceeds 0x10000, so a chunk holds at most 64 KB; 2. copies the bytes when the stored length is at least the length (a stored chunk); 3. otherwise checks that OodleLZDecoder MemorySizeNeeded(8 = Kraken, length) fits its 0x20800-byte work buffer and calls OodleLZ Decompress (fuzz-safe) from oo2core 5 win64.dll , asserting "Decompression failure." unless exactly length bytes come out; 4. skips to the next 4-byte boundary. In the sample, 638,807 chunks were packed and 31,098 stored. Packed chunks start with the Oodle block bytes 8C 06 (5,287 of 5,910 sampled) or 8C 02 (623). The first chunk of every one of the 488,752 entries decodes with the shipped DLL. Over the whole install the stored data is 62.8% of its unpacked size.

Every file starts with a 4-character tag, and the extension decides it: across all 488,752 records each extension maps to one format ( .txt aside). x: The game's data lives in one database, database\game\game.gamedb , stored in hotchunk.arch06 (56,759,100 bytes; see Archives and file formats). The file stores each distinct string, float pair and vector once, and every cell that holds that value points at the same bytes; loading keeps the sharing. The 166,606 float-pair cells point at 3,071 distinct pairs: (0, 0) is shared by 72,774 cells across the database, (1, 1) by 17,492, (100, 200) by 13,591, (0.25, 0.25) by 13,257 and (0, 200) by 10,743. The 50,734 vector cells point at 2,596 distinct vectors, one all-zero vector serving 25,616 cells. Writing the floats behind such a pointer changes every field that shares them; storing a different pointer in one cell changes that field alone.

In the file a link is (category ordinal << 20) index , where the ordinal is the category's position in the hash-sorted table (the loaded header's +0x2C ) and the index counts the category's primaries first, then its secondaries. 0xFFFFFFFF is null; 0 is a real link (category 0, primary 0). In memory the cell holds the target's header address. In the running game 5,204,006 link cells hold 3,471,923 nulls (0xFFFFFFFF in the file, every one), 1,316,316 pointers to secondaries and 415,767 to primaries, and none point anywhere else. t: Changing values in a running game
x: - A cell is plain memory: the getters read it on every call, with no lock, checksum or cache in between (the fast getters above are the whole read path). Whether a change is seen is decided by the readers' copies above. - Only the cells a record's own run claims belong to it: a field with count 0 has no cell, and an element written past a field's count lands in another field of the same record, or past the instance in the next record. - A Bool shares its word with up to 31 others; a whole-cell write changes all of them. - A StringEnum cell takes P919 of the enum name; a String, Int64, float-pair or vector cell takes a pointer, and the bytes it points at are shared by every cell with the same value. - A RecordLink cell accepts any record: neither the getters nor the cell know the declared target, so nothing stops a link to a record of the wrong category, and its consumer reads that record with the declared type's layout.

- Apart from the AudioHooks records, which the audio thread compiles at load, which categories are read off the main thread (render, audio, input polling, animation jobs), so that a change can race its reader? Camera, interface world-UI, audio control values, input profiles, native wildlife, AI sensors and the weather and lighting structures are the candidates; sampling the field readers per thread, or tracing their callers to the thread routines, would settle it. - Do loads rebuild record instances from the file? A changed cell can return to the file's value after a loading screen, yet changed cells can also survive a region change; whether a load re-reads the instance block, and on which path, is not traced. - The loader tests a gamedb patch path and the byte 0x266CD70. t: World: regions, layers, placements and world objects
x: A region's world is a set of world parts , each streamed in as a section and turned into a world context full of placed objects. This chapter describes the parts on disk, the streamer that loads them, the objects they create and the world data that the rest of the engine queries.

The game has eight regions. Each has one main part ( worlds\retail\<folder \<folder , the only part with terrain) and a set of layers under worlds\retail\<folder \sectionsandlayers\ : story and side content, fortress pieces, lighting and its per-Overlord variants. 1,303 layers ship (each identified by the paths its own container lists, never by its archive entry name): Folder Region Layers --- --- --- volcano Gorgoroth 243 snowmtn Seregost 239 island Nurnen 228 mtnpass Cirith Ungol 228 desert Lithlad 221 minasithil Minas Ithil 138 blackgates the Black Gate 4 baraddur Barad-dur 2 Seven regions have a region archive and a lighting archive ( <folder .arch06 , <folder lighting.arch06 ), and the patch archives add and replace parts. Lithlad has neither: its main part and all 221 of its layers are in the patch archives (the containers in Patch DLC4 , with standalone .objres and .scripts copies in later patches). A world part is an EMBB container (see Archives and file formats). Every layer carries its own prefab ( .inst ), and 1,302 of 1,303 carry the same eight further parts, named after the layer: .objres (the object registry below), .terrain , .hkai (navigation mesh), .wldclnt (static

The name registrar 0x4DBF08 either copies the name (and sets +0xDE to 1) or keeps a pointer into the part's strings ( +0xDE = 0), hashes it into the node at +0x28 and calls the context's vf10 0x4DBF78, which picks the bucket ( hash & 0x7FF , 0x4DBF84) and appends the node at the tail (0x115ED3C, which asserts "Error: Adding a link that is already inside of a list" only when the node itself is already linked). Duplicate names are legal : nothing checks the name. The lookup 0x4DC078 compares the hash and then the name case-insensitively, walking from the tail, so the newest object of a name answers. Render and collision are bound by name. The component build (vtable +0x68 - 0x333430) asks the context's vf5 0x3334F0, which looks the registered name ( +0x40 ) up in the context's resource table ( ctx+0x98 ). An object created under a name its part does not list gets no render component and no physics; created under an existing object's name it receives that object's model and collision. Because the newest object answers a name, the members of a prefab created after the original members bind to each other during post-create.

A script's Create does not construct anything: the objects already exist in the part before any script runs, and scripts bind to them by name. The <Class .Create(scriptId, name, b3, relative) stubs of 117 of 125 script classes share 0x5013A8 - 0x501B64, which composes the name (a . prefix or relative prepends the prefab instance's name) and calls the object server's vf14 with the scriptId's own context; the lookup is not given the class. A missing name or a class mismatch returns Class.None ; ScriptObject.Create is a function of its own, 0x501CAC. A scriptId is {PrefabName, PropertyName, Instance} ; Instance is a weak handle (prefab instance at payload +0x48 ) that becomes null when the prefab's part streams out.

GameBase:CopyXForm(A, B) 0x1823B70 is SetPosition(A, B+0xAC) 0x1454EC followed by SetRotation(A, B+0xB8) 0xEF690; render state and spatial structures follow the setters, and it works across contexts. Collision follows ownership : the setter path 0x274C3C forwards to the physics body at +0x98 , so only pieces the object owns move. 3,382 of 3,491 FireProp s own no pieces (their collision is baked into the part's static PhysicsBSP ), so a moved bench or barrel stack keeps its old collision; DynamicObjectGroupBrush es (607 of 634) and cage brushes (vt 0x1FA3C00, 84 of 84) own theirs and stay solid where they go. A destructible prop is a prefab of sibling objects (brush, explosion, effects, nav obstacle, volume controller): moving one member leaves the others behind.

Objects live and die with their part's context. When the part streams again its objects are created again from the file, so a moved object is back at its authored transform and an object created into that context is gone. Nothing about placed objects is saved. A class's destructor is at +0x20 of its static descriptor.

Cages, nests, barrels, gates and traps are dynamic object groups : a DynamicObjectGroup object (the root) with DynamicObjectGroupBrush members (the breakable or interactive geometry), DynamicObjectGroupState members named after their states ( Barre 46.DOGS Fire , WaspN 03.DOGS Shoot ) and the prefab's effects. The brushes bind the group's composite prefab ( caragorcage , waspnest , ghulcloset : no draws of their own) and sit at fixed offsets from the root (35 of 35, 53 of 53 and 226 of 226 in those three); the drawn art is the prefab's children at the root's transform. t: Building the grid: KILL and CUT volumes
x: QueueRebuild 0x2BB1C8 files each row by its transform (full rotation, translation only, identity). The build 0x2BA9F8 first instances every owner's two volume lists (planes transformed by 0x2BB01C, {A, B} copied, covered cells flagged), then inserts every line through 0x257C70: - List 1 = KILL. The engine calls these volumes MarkupKiller (4 to 64 cutting planes, asserted in 0x694AC4; the editor class is MarkupKillerBrush ). A line that touches an applicable kill volume is dropped whole. - List 2 = CUT. 0x2582F8 removes the part of a line inside an applicable cut volume; the outside pieces survive if they are at least 25 cm long (the constant 0x267A4D8, compared squared: grid +0x28 = 625). Uncut lines keep any length (20,199 live lines are under 25 cm). - Which volumes apply (0x258280): a volume applies to a line unless the line belongs to the volume's own owner (same A) or both have the same nonzero cut group. A line with A = 0 is never touched. A disabled owner's cut volumes are still built (125 of 1,051), but its own lines are hidden from queries. Measured in a running game (two reads with the world re-streamed between them; 186,023 and 184,993 lines): no line lies more than 1 cm

t: Scripting: HavokScript, world scripts and natives

x: The game's scripts run on HavokScript , Havok's fork of Lua 5.1 with typed structures ( hstructure declarations, hmake constructors) and light-userdata literals ( 0x572b96b9hi ); its standard library table is at 0x21DAEB0 and the source compiler ships in the executable. The main VM is [GM+0x6CE8] - a CScriptVM (vt 0x230EF00) whose +0x58 is the lua State : L+0x10 the global state ( +0x560 compiler settings, +0x588 the panic handler 0x1CFEEB4), L+0x48 / +0x50 the stack top and base; stack slots are 16 bytes {u32 tag, value} . - CreateVM 0x1CFE890 and SetupVM 0x1CFEBCC build a VM; RegisterAllScriptBindings 0x1C01778 registers every native, the per-type binder 0x1B9F69C registers the DB record types (see GameDB), and a helper 0x1D87644 registers into the main VM through the global script agent [GM+0x6CF0] . - LoadBuffer 0x55B920(L, compiler settings, ...) and Pcall 0x406344 run a chunk. - Natives do not validate their arguments, and engine asserts write to a null address, so a native called with an argument shape the shipped scripts never use can fault.

A script names a record as DB<Kind .Name ; the lookup ( WBDBRecordLookup ) takes the kind's live category and the name's hash and binary-searches the category (0x278540). The Lua names differ from the category paths: DBFX / DBFXSeq ( Client/ClientFXList / ClientFXSequence ), DBCombatBuff , DBMaterialState ( Combat/FX/MaterialController/States , 168 records), DBSlowMo (332), DBAlignments (52), DBBandType , DBCombatAppliedState , DBCharacterModels . A native's argument types are visible in its stub: each record argument is fetched as mov rdx, [rip+X]; call 0x407BAC , where [X] holds the live category of the expected kind (checked on 27 of 27 natives). Most DEBUG bindings are stripped (no implementation, or the empty stub 0x5009B0). Script calls into the engine fall in two groups: calls that set engine state or queue work (weather, material states, AI requests: AISpawnManager:SummonGrunts only queues a spawn request) and calls that dispatch to script listeners - System:ActivateRemoteScript is the script bus's Notify 0x605990, which calls the global script agent per listener and so belongs on the main thread.

The engine keeps a stack of the scripts it is running: depth u32 [base+0x2702540] , entries 0x277C1B0 + i 0x80 (at most 16; depth 0 is the static 0x2680000), entry +0x28 = the running script's name. 0x503EF8 returns the top entry's name. Only the engine pushes: the eventmap dispatcher 0x406538 (push 0x4066B8 - 0x5029D0 - 0x502A00 - 0x502A44, which always writes a name, "Invalid" at worst; pop 0x406744 - 0x115F8E0) and the resource loaders 0x4FD9C0, 0x4FEFA8 and 0x4A6088. A few natives require it: NPC::SetAlignment 0x7D2ED4 asserts "This function should only be called from script code" when the name is empty; the other direct users of the name are CPlayerObj::SetAISpectatorInvisible , the player's SetHidden (vf32, logging only), SetRetreatingEnabled 0x1BAE1F8, 0x1BA7C8C and 0x1D86F28. Such natives work only from inside an engine-dispatched script handler; LoadBuffer + Pcall push nothing.

Every world layer's script is one SCRI payload: "SCRI" u32 version (1) u8 flag u32 length body flag 1 = Lua source text, flag 0 = HavokScript bytecode ("\x1bLua" + header) It ships as a standalone <layer .scripts archive entry (the patch archives ship these, and the standalone copy wins) and / or as a SCRI section inside the layer's container. A layer's chunk ends with G.loadedresource = section <hash ; its entries are script threads function(self, threadId, scriptId) that may LithThreadSleep(threadId, seconds) . Objects named .SC are StartupCommand s whose <prefab SC Script <hash entry the engine starts as a thread. Script threads run on simulation time, so they wait while the game is paused or unfocused. Compiled layer scripts are cached for the whole process in the main VM's global reinstall (0x6A60EC: reinstall[id] unset - compile the buffer and set it; set - reuse it), so a layer's script is compiled once per process, the first time its region loads. Which object runs which script is world data: the layer's ScriptBind block maps objects and events to functions of the layer's own script (see World).

The interpreter. The main loop 0x1D88000 fetches a u32 instruction, takes op = insn 25 , refuses op 0x5B and jumps through a 92-entry table at 0x1D8B208. Two further interpreter functions start at 0x1D8B378 and 0x1D8E188, each with a 61-case dispatch of its own. The callers (0x6C8E38, 0x406C94) pick one by the mode word of the VM's global state [[L+0x10]+0x1C8] : 0 runs the main loop, 1 runs 0x1D8B378 and 2 runs 0x1D8E188. The main VM runs in mode 0. Fields: A = bits 0-7 (a register, or a flag for EQ / LT / LE / TEST); C = bits 8-16 (RK: 256 and above = constant K[C - 256]); B = bits 17-24, with bit 25 set by the BK opcode of a pair (B is then a constant index); Bx = bits 8-24; sBx = Bx - 0xFFFF, relative to the next instruction. DATA (op 76) is a word the VM skips; several opcodes own a fixed number of DATA words after them (inline caches, structure ids, SETLIST counts). NEWSTRUCT's DATA word holds the structure id. return f(x) compiles to TAILCALL followed by an unreachable RETURN A, 0 , and jumps are threaded (an inner else skip or a break lands directly on the enclosing construct's destination). t: The main thread's loop and the window pump
x: The main loop is 0xC25568: it calls the application object [base+0x26FEFD8] (vt 0x1FFE760) slot 33 ( +0x108 ) and slot 29 ( +0xE8 ), then pumps window messages ( PeekMessageW / DispatchMessageW at 0xC2589A) and runs a sleep limiter. The game window belongs to the main thread. The main thread's frame wait (slot 28 0x380FAC - 0x38105C - 0x1CF430) is back-pressure for space in the render command ring and pumps messages too (0x6EE5D0, dispatch 0x6EE670); both pumps share the re-entrancy byte 0x277DBB0. Posting to the render ring (0x381FCC posts {0x1EE088, context, function} ) uses an unlocked bump allocation, so only the main thread may post.
- What sets interpreter modes 1 and 2 ( [[L+0x10]+0x1C8] ), and where the INTRINSIC opcodes are executed.

t: Rendering: the D3D11 layer, passes, shaders and lighting
x: The renderer is a deferred Direct3D 11 renderer that runs on its own thread as a command processor: the main thread records each frame into a command ring and the render thread replays it. How the ring works, the order of one frame's commands, where the render thread's time goes and how a frame is presented are in Threads and the frame ; this chapter covers what the renderer does with the GPU.

The engine keeps its Direct3D objects in one static block at 0x272D1C0: Offset Address Meaning --- --- --- +0x00 0x272D1C0 the ID3D11Device (138 code references; stored once per interface version) +0x20 0x272D1E0 a render-device object (vt 0x1FFC508) whose +0x08 is the next row +0x28 0x272D1E8 the device context the world renderer calls : 450 reads in 96 functions +0x58 0x272D218 the immediate context created with the device (one reader, at shutdown) +0x60 .. +0x98 DXGI objects; +0x88 the swap chain +0xA8 0x272D268 the presented-frame counter The object at +0x28 answers the ID3D11DeviceContext interface: after mov rcx, [0x272D1E8] the code calls slots +0x40, +0xC8, +0xF8, +0x1D8, +0x1F8, +0x218 with the same (0, count, views) arguments, which are the six shader stages' SetShaderResources . Three engine objects keep their own copy of the device pointer (vt 0x22C5F50 +0xB0 , vt 0x230CBE0 +0xA8 , vt 0x230CBA0 +0x28 ); none keeps a copy of the context, so every world draw goes through the static handle. The user interface does not use this path. Flash menus and the HUD draw through Scaleform GFx 's own renderer, Render::HAL (vt 0x2002498, 166 slots; 18 of them open a profiler scope nam

The renderer is deferred. The G-buffer pixel shaders write four targets: Target Format Contents --- --- --- 0 R10G10B10A2 normals: bits 0-19 the bumped normal's offset, bits 20-31 the geometric normal 1 RGBA8 diffuse albedo (bytes 0-2) 2 RGBA8 specular: byte 0 roughness (the lighting uses r r ), byte 1 specular occlusion, byte 2 reflectance (above 0.667 = metal) 3 RGBA8 material: alpha bits 28-31 = the lighting class The lighting is a compute pass ( lighting\tiledlighting.fxo ) that reads the normal, specular and material targets as UAVs and branches on the class: 0 standard, 1 hair (a Marschner model), 2 subsurface / emissive . Its sun term is GGX; dielectrics use a fixed F0 of 0.04, and image-based light comes from split-sum probes sampled at mip 6 sqrt(roughness) . There is no screen-space reflection in the lighting. The work is tiled. Each frame the main thread issues 13 tile updates ( BufferTileIndices 0x1791CC with 0x247108) and one indirect draw of light volumes as icosahedra ( DrawIcosahedronInstancesIndirect , 0x6C74A8). The global shader constants (below) name the rest of the structure: screen tiles sorted by the kind of sun shadow they need into separate job queues ( k R

translucent\overlay\rainandfireoverlay.fxo is a full-screen pass that runs after the G-buffer and before the lighting. It reads and rewrites all four G-buffer targets as UAVs, so it changes every surface it covers: terrain, buildings, characters and gear. It rebuilds each pixel's world position from depth ( t0 ), reads the world normal ( t1 ; up is t1.y ), and owns: - wetness: the global wetness cb3[3].z lerps roughness toward the wet target cb3[4].x ; on level ground (up above 0.97) the bump is scaled to 15% before animated ripples are added; - an animated raindrop-impact mask from time-scrolled noise ( t4 ) that roughens, darkens and lowers reflectance where a drop lands, faded out beyond 75 m; - a roof-occlusion compare map ( t6 , matrices cb2[28..31] ) used by the rain branch within 75 m, so covered ground stays dry. The renderable behind it is the class vt 0x1FFECD8, which receives three render commands per frame (0x70C0E0, 0x7146A0, 0x72FDE0). Its parameters come from its material, rainandfireoverlay.mat , and from the weather (below). The pass belongs to the world view: menu scenes such as the army screen do not run it.

lighting\fogoverlay.fxo runs after lighting. It reads the lit scene and rewrites it as scene transmittance + inscatter (depth t0.x , the lit scene t3 , view-to-world cb2[4..6] ; its vertex shader builds the view ray from cb2[21] and the texture coordinate from cb2[22] ). Because fog is added after lighting, distant surfaces take the fog's colour whatever their albedo. The render thread registers the fog material ( fog overlay.mat ) during its own initialisation.

Shaders ship as compiled .fxo files, addressed by tree path ( lighting\tiledlighting.fxo , solid\nemesis\gear lod0.fxo , translucent\overlay\rainandfireoverlay.fxo ...). A shader file holds variants: the orc gear shaders ( solid\nemesis\gear lod0 , lod1 , alphatest lod0 , alphatest lod1 ), which every orc shares, each carry three pixel-shader variants, skeletal, mesh type 4 (dithered fade: it discards where the dither value exceeds 1 - cb3[13].w ) and mesh type 5 (which blends reflectance toward four constant specular tints). Talion's gear uses its own trees ( talion armor , detail , armornocull , cloth , weapon , hair , ring ...); talion armor is one pixel shader whose output reflectance above 0.667 marks metal.

Every loaded shader tree, the renderer's own and every material's, hangs in one static hash table at 0x27AEC38 : 128 buckets of 0x18 bytes {first, last, self} (each bucket points at itself, so a bucket is recognisable), and the bucket is StringHash(tree path) & 127 . A node is: Offset Field --- --- +0x00 / +0x08 next / previous (the chain ends back at the bucket) +0x10 the tree path's hash (equal to the resource's +0x20 ) +0x30 the shader tree object in use +0x38, +0x50 the resource There is one node per material and draw state, not one per tree: Talion's armour shader had 33 nodes, his weapon 8, his cloth 8, his head 8. Walking one bucket finds every node of a shader. A material loaded later gets new nodes on the same tree. Tree names carry a content hash.

t: Visual effects: ClientFX data and runtime
x: Every visual effect - sparks, fire, blood, auras, light flares, screen effects, camera shakes and effect sounds - is a ClientFX effect: an .fxp file holding a small GameDB database of nodes, played by an effect manager as instances.

CGameClientShell [base+0x26FFA98] +0xA98 Simulation +0xAA0 RealTime +0xAA8 PlayerTime +0xAB0 CompanionTime +0xAB8 WorldUI (unique ptr - manager wrapper, 0x18358 bytes, vt 0x22F3178; global list [base+0x26C6A98]) +-- +0x28 inner manager (vt 0x1F67400, 0x18330 bytes) +0xB8 vector of 0x28-byte entries -- entry +0x18 -- effect instance (vt 0x1DAB360, pool 0x2A3E9A8) +0x230 FxResource (0x60) - keys - node types +0x220 KeyData block - one object per node +0x128 background work list -- FXBackgroundThread GameManager +0x6DB0 = the FX thread object (routine 0x116B11C) GameManager +0x6DB8 = the FX performance / budget manager (ClientFxPerfMgr.cpp)

An .fxp starts with LTFX and version 8, followed by a GameDB database ( FxGlobalProps and one record per node). The magic occurs exactly once in the executable, in the loader 0x48FBB90: it reads 8 bytes from a stream, checks LTFX and version 8, allocates the 0x60-byte FxResource , reads the database from the stream (0x74CF10) into FxResource+0x48 , and fails with "Failed to load the database out of a stream." The loader is vf3 and the processor vf4 0x3E4540 of the effect resource handler (vt 0x2312410); path resolution happens upstream, so the loader only sees a stream. The file ends with a u32: the count of the database's (u32, u32) pair table ( db+0x68 ), 0 in all 968 shipped effects checked. A file without it makes the body reader 0x4B9B50 read 4 bytes past the end (0x4B9C60), which stalls the resource loader (see Resource streaming). The database's categories are sorted by the hash of their path, and the loader binary-searches them (0x115B4D4). Running the engine's own load and processing on every shipped effect in an emulator, 968 of 968 read to their last byte and 949 are accepted; the 19 others are placeholders with an empty key list, which the processor refuses by design. Ragdolls are a death effect. Every character model carries a physics ragdoll, but the powered ragdoll, its brain and the joint tuning from the database are started only by the dead-body step 0x2F8460: the slot claim (0x65C214), the brain start (0x65C274) and the joint setup (0x64D4A4) each have that one caller. Knockdowns and other reactions of living characters are animations.

The NPC Update runs its dead-body branch, slot 121 (base implementation 0x175020), once the combat object's dead byte [char+0x26A8]+0x4A0 and the byte char+0x225E are set (see Threads and the frame); on the frame of death the AI update itself calls the step once. 0x2F8460(state = char+0x1AF0 , character): 1. Reads Combat/Category.RagdollReaction of the killing attack (0x65E990; 11 of 2,559 categories set one) and, when a ragdoll is pending, its InitalVelocityScale and ForceValue . 2. Claims a ring slot, then, when the character's model ( [char+0x2B30] ) names a Character/Models.RagdollConfig , applies that config's joints, enables the ragdoll and starts its brain; otherwise it starts the controller with no config and no brain. 3. Fires Combat/Buffs.DeathProjectiles , switches the character to RigidBody , plays the clip named by Character/Models/Global.RagdollDeathAnimation ( base ) on the model and posts the audio hook CharacterSwitchesToRagdoll . 4. On every later frame: runs the brain (0x30F6D4), then tests for rest. Counting from the state's time stamp and leaving out the brain's running time, a body is at rest after 15 s, or after 3 s once its speed falls below Character/Models

Physics is Havok Physics 2016.2 ( hk2016 2 0 r1 ) in its new pipeline: the hknp classes, which replaced the older hkp API. The build is a hybrid: rigid bodies are hknp , but ragdoll constraints are still the legacy hkpRagdollConstraintData and hkpLimitedHingeConstraintData . Havok AI ( hkai ) provides navigation meshes, avoidance and silhouettes, and Havok Cloth deforms cloth with hkaSkeleton ; Havok Animation and Behavior are not used (see Animation). HavokScript runs the game's scripts (see Scripting). Havok work runs on three HavokWorkerThread s (shared routine 0x11AFE58) and on the main thread's task queue: in play the main thread spends about 5% of its time in the physics step ( TtPhysics , 0x6528B8) and about 3% in the Havok task queue, where hkaiAvoidanceSolverTask shows up.

The world has exactly one construction path (its constructor 0x15464FC has one caller, 0x11B1504, whose only caller is 0x1187004), and the engine publishes its owner in a static slot: [base+0x2A86760] the physics owner (0x6860 bytes), published by 0x1186FB0 (1 write, 66 reads in 60 functions) [base+0x2A86768] u32 generation, incremented at each publish owner+0x20 - hknpWorld (allocated from the Havok heap, 0xAA0 bytes) The world is rebuilt on every world load.

Crows, bats, seagulls and the desert raptors are not characters. Each is an AvianObject (vt 0x1DBBD30, 0x518 bytes, derived from the generic game object, without a character controller, behaviour graph or inventory) spawned by a placed world object, an AvianMarker (vt 0x1FA4CD0). A marker owns at most one bird.

Avian/Definition holds 14 species records: Crow, Crow Eat, bat, bat Day, bat DaySleep, bat AnyTime, Seagul, Seagull Eat, raptor Desert, raptor Desert Day, raptor Desert Night, raptor Desert Night Clear, testing and testingBenchmark. A definition names the model ( Model.Cha Crow , Cha Bat , Cha Seagull , Cha RaptorDesert ), a scale range (crows 1.0-1.5, the others 0.9-1.1), a weather / time-of-day predicate ( Weather/Predicates/Forecast.AnyTimeNoRain , NightNoRain , DayNoWeather ...), a combat tree ( Hunting Crow , Hunting Bat , Hunting Seagull , Hunting Avian ), a render-ID setup, seven animation slots each with a weighted variant list (perched, eating, take-off, bank left, bank right, flap, landing), perch and flight durations (average and variance), take-off height and distance, climb, descent, turn and lateral rates, a death effect, a respawn time and the group-sound settings. A crow perches 9 +/- 6 s and flies 60 +/- 11 s; bats fly 900 s; every species respawns after 33-120 s.

t: AI: planning, perception, spawning and group combat
x: Every NPC runs one update per frame that selects a target, aims, moves and ticks a tree of planner steps whose priority order decides its behaviour. NPCs enter the world as requests queued on the spawn manager, made by ambient spawners, scripts and summons, and resolved from a spawn channel to a template, a model and a character type.

The plan tree is built once, at character set-up, from the NPC's AI/CharacterTypes.PlanTree record (accessor 0x7279C0): vt 0x1FB3640::vf12 0x3FA718 - 0x45AFDC - 0x6FC774 - 0x6FC7B8 - ... - the step factory 0x45CEE8 (2,800 bytes). The factory recurses (0x45CEE8 - 0x45C724 - 0x45CEB0 - 0x45CEE8), so composite steps build their children. 0x45AFDC stores the result at [npc+0x2D38] by move-assignment (0x75F2DC); the old tree is freed by 0x3EB630. If the character type has no PlanTree , the brain lookup returns null and the creator frees the new object (see Spawning).

An affix's value is FloatIndex.IndexedValues[ItemLevel - 1] of its VariableMin table (10 of 10 checked live). A sword's "Melee Attack" is the affix 1Sword Base Prop <rarity or set - Float DmgMod M FLAT (level 80: Common 160, Epic 166, Legendary 169); the player's own Float DmgBase M BASE is 0, so the sword's roll is the whole flat input to the player's melee damage formula ( DmgForm Plyr Melee ). Unequipping subtracts the current values, so an affix value changed while the item is equipped leaves the stat table out of step. The engine's own upgrade (0xFBAAC0, at 0xFBB2EC: strip, level = min(owner level + 1, 80) , recompute) removes, changes and re-applies. x: Every named orc, olog and story character is a FactionMember owned by the faction system, seated in an army's rows, and changed by faction events that the engine applies to it. The hierarchy, the promotions, the returns from death and the ambushes are data: rows, events and reward lists in the Faction/ categories of the GameDB, driven by a small set of engine functions. Traits, classes and personalities are in Captain traits, classes and personalities; story characters, betrayal scenes and region ownership in Quests, story and scenes; looks in Captain appearance; what a save keeps in Saves, the store and the network layer.

The FactionMember (vt 0x1FD5EA0) is 0x528 bytes . Both allocation sites ask for 0x528 bytes (0x19ED468: mov ecx,0x528 - allocator 0x3DE238 - constructor 0x1BB4C1C; 0xF99FF0 likewise) and the constructor's last store is +0x520 . The name is a string id, FM+0x170 . 0x1BC6040(fm, id) stores it, looks up the localized UTF-16 string, converts it with WideCharToMultiByte on the system ANSI code page ( CodePage 0, Windows-1252 on a Western system) and copies at most 31 characters into the 32-byte buffer FM+0x498 ; an id of 0 clears the buffer. FM+0x4B8 is stored 0-based; the game shows it plus one, and caps the shown level at 85. SetLevel 0x35188C ends in 0x353C44, which sets flag bits 30 and 31 when the level reaches two thresholds read from the army; crossing the second with no tribe assigns one (0x1BC6718, reason "XPLevel"). - From the seats. For each army context, each runtime row and each column, a seat value other than -1 is a pool index into the army's pool object ( ctx+0x20 ). Each member can hold a cooldown table [FM+0x258] : a 0x18-byte object {entries, u32 count, category} of {record, u32 expiry turn} entries, the category being Faction/Events/SimEventCooldown ( [base+0x2701A18] ; two records, PowerStruggle CD and HuntingMission CD ). The gate 0x1BC0C2C(fm, SimEvent.RequiredCooldown ) passes when there is no table or the entry has expired, and refuses when the table exists but has no entry (the lookup 0x1BBC410 returns null). The setter 0x1BB7578 creates and sizes a table (0x1BBF840) only when none exists. The FactionMember loader creates the table when the save flags one (0x1BC0F2C) but never sizes it, and reads each saved entry into a temporary (0x1BC0EC4). After a load, every member that had a cooldown is refused power struggles and hunts permanently: in a late-campaign pool of 500, no table was sized and 60 living seated captains carried an empty one. An emulated generation pass on Minas Ithil's army, with every captain free and no events, refused 204 of 221 attempts; every power-struggle and hunt candidate (340 of 340) failed at this gate, the rest at their campaign gates.

Death and return run through the kill path and events: 1. Mark. The kill path 0x6DB95C (0x1BB9F84 for event kills) stores the death's Faction/Resurrection record at FM+0x2C0 and, when the row has ResurrectionEnabled , rolls the odds (0x6DBD4C: presets refused, row, predicate, odds table). On success the evaluator 0x1BC5D44 picks a fitting scar (0x1B5AA00; none = "No Available Scars", nothing changes), increments FS+0x21C and FM+0x500 , sets bit 4, stores the scar at FM+0x348 (unless it equals FM+0x370 ) and fires the record's DeathEvent through 0x40C0AC. Without ResurrectionEnabled the kill path resets the mock member (0x6DBCFC). 2. Queue. t: Story and DLC characters in the hierarchy
x: A story character is a Faction/PresetMembers record (203; 67 belong to the DLCs). The saves of the base campaign hold the DLC cast too: the mercenary army, the ten Blade of Galadriel twin armies and their presets (the Nazgul sisters DLC3 Nazgul Twin 1 , eight DLC3ToMain specialists, DLC FakeDarkTalion , DLC4 Desert Overlord ). The base game's Nazgul are presets as well (six GP Nazgul ). The build sequence is in Quests, story and scenes; the seating law is the creator's: The creator seats any preset by its FactionRow . 0x1C1D378(ctx, preset) allocates (0x1C23C10), builds (0x1BC06C0: +0x190 = the preset, +0x3A0 = 0, +0x520 = 3, flag 25) and registers the member (0x61B5E8). With no row he is rowless at NoRowXPLevel - 1 (0x1C21448). With a row he is levelled for it (0x1C1BDA8), the column is the preset's FactionColumn (0x1C206AC); if that seat is taken (0x4F9014) or the column is negative, the row (0x61AC00) gives a free column (0x1C1BEB4), and the seat call 0x61E13C(flag 1) runs only when a free column exists : in a full row the character is built but unseated. Then each preset event is fired through 0x40C0AC. Its callers are army initialisation 0xFDAC54 (the definition's PresetMember

FM+0x51A is the intel level (0-3 in play), and FM+0x510 the intel mask that 0x62136C rebuilds from it with the army's InterrogationSetup ( Default , three DataStages ): level 0 gives 0x2, level 1 0x9B, levels 2 and 3 0xFB (3, 30 and 531 of 564 members). Mask bit 0 means the name is known; UnlockName 0x621208 sets it. The Army screen draws a generic model ( Character/Models/HierarchyUnknown ) for a member whose name is not known and who has never killed the player (see User interface). A level-0 start is ordinary: the builder build, 0x1BC00C8, 0x1BC02AC, the preset build (twice) and System::HierarchyResetPreSetMemberData 0x1C2373C force it, and the war simulation (0xFCD340, 0xFD0660) forces it whenever its level is lower. The hierarchy treats bit 21 (mock dead) as eliminated: the henchmen link effects 0x18316FC / 0x183191C skip such a member.

t: Captain appearance: bodies, armour, colour and scars

SetPieceSlot(appearance, slot, piece, design, visual) returns early when the slot already holds that piece; otherwise it removes the old piece's appearance tags (0x4C64EC), adds the new piece's (0x4C647C), writes the design into its cell, and, when a visual is passed, swaps the piece on that visual as well.

Every member build runs the same sequence: 1. Parameters. 0x577190 clears a parameter block and 0x1BEA190 fills it from the member: +0x00 the seed FM+0x168 , +0x250 a size fraction (below), +0x210 the class model FM+0x278 , +0x228 personality, +0x238 role, +0x240 row (a story character's DisplayFactionRow when he has none), the active traits, and the class kit's appearance-tag setup from the combat tree FM+0x188 (0x576FFC). 2. Items. 0x1C10F00 empties the inventory (0x1C7BF4: every slot, the colour list and the look-record list), then 0x1C10AB0 gives, in order, the personality's Items , the role's Item list, the role's ScarType items, the tribe's Item list and the class kit's ItemsFactionMember , then the kit's named list for a follower ( Named PlayerFollowerItems ) or an enemy ( Named SauronFollowerItems ), chosen by flag bit 27. 4. Every roll of the look derives from the 64-bit seed FM+0x168 : Lcg(s) = s 0xBB38435 + 0x3619636B Unit(s) = (u32)(s 32) / 4294967295.0 The size fraction is Unit(Lcg(seed)) (plus 0.0). 0x4C5194 copies the seed once and passes that copy to the body roll 0x6A9F38, the head pick 0x2EDBB4, the helmet pick 0x701A98, the hair pick 0x6C8BB4, the colour roll 0x2E9A2C and the accessory picks 0x6F4CA4 / 0x6F5614, in that order; every draw advances it. A class whose body table draws a different number of times therefore also changes the face, hair and colours that follow. Item builds start again from the seed: the give path passes FM+0x168 to the item build, which draws from a local copy, so a member draws the same design from the same builder at every build. Colour items ( FlairColors ) are rolled from the seed the same way. The army outfit's choice of slots is the exception: it draws from the engine's global generator (0x1B3C6C). The weighted pick used throughout is the reservoir 0x1B3B90: a weight of zero or less never draws; otherwise s = Lcg(s) , r = Unit(s) (acc + w) , the entry wins when w r , and acc += w .

0x6A9F38 walks Model/SimpleModel.Models ( StructuresModelSimpleModelEntry ). For each entry, the weight is the BodyWeights[j] of the last RequiredScaleRange[j] (a float pair) that contains the size fraction; an entry with no matching range or no Body.Model is skipped. The chosen entry's BodyType goes to +0x00 and its Body to piece slot 0. The orc classes' tables: Class Buff (3) Slim (2) Stocky (4) --- --- --- --- Orc Infantry 1 over 0.3 - 0.7 1 over 0 - 0.33 1 over 0.67 - 1 Orc Defender 0.3 over 0 - 0.6 0 1 over 0 - 1 Orc Berserker 1 over 0 - 1 0 0.15 over 0.6 - 1 Orc Spearman 0.15 over 0.3 - 0.7 1 over 0 - 1 0 Orc Archer 0.15 over 0.3 - 0.7 1 over 0 - 1 0.01 over 0.67 - 1 OlogHai Infantry has one entry (body type 5). A Defender is Buff for about 14% of seeds (0.6 x 0.3 / 1.3); a Spearman or an Archer is mostly Slim. The bodies are Orc Buff Body001 , Orc Slim Body001 and Orc Stk Body001V2 . Changing a member's class therefore re-rolls his body at the next build, and a non-orc class gives a non-orc body and head.

The in-world size uses the same fraction. 0x7F8488(fm) takes the army ( FM+0x180 , else FM+0x178 ), the seed and the class, and 0x4E541C returns size = min + (max - min) Unit(Lcg(seed)) + army.ScaleAdditiveModifier with (min, max) the class's Character/Models.AIScaleRange ( Faction MtnPass adds 0.1). 0x4E3CF0 stores it into the character's scale component ( char+0x2738 , at +0x10 and +0x6C ) only when it differs by more than 0.01. Because body and size share the fraction, an Infantry captain is Slim at the small end of his class's size range, Buff in the middle and Stocky at the large end.

The base model ( +0x20 ) does not change with it; 16 of the 70 body pieces are built for orc anim base . Body designs are the nine of armour slot 10 ( AD Body Scar , AD Machine Body , AD Glutton Body , AD Infested Body , AD Tinder Body , AD Flint Body , AD Dragonborn Body , AD BodyModel Forced Buff ...). - A painted skin is a texture on the same mesh: a builderless item <Name BodyPaint whose MaterialSetVariants swap the body piece's material set. Model/SimpleModelMaterialSetVariant (58 records) holds six body families (Digger, BlackBlade, Gravewalker, Unashamed, Rogue, Slave), each a variant for Buff and Slim (excluding Tag Olog and Tag Stk ), a Stk one and a LOD one; Slave has no Stocky variant. The build gives only the role's ScarType ; nothing in it reads FM+0x370 , and its item clear removes the earlier scar items, so a rebuild drops a scar given by AddScar . The scars a death or a return brings are in The Nemesis system. By their items: Poison, Branded Slave and Mauled (and the Olog Poison) bare the head (an AD empty head item in armour slot 0); Metal Head and Sack Head replace the head (armour slot 11) and MetalJaw Helmet uses slot 9; ExposedBrain, DaggerHead and AxeHead are helmets; burns, cuts, eye

Tags are added by SetPieceSlot , by item equip (0x61B868, an item's AppearanceTags ), by the class kit at the start of a build and by colour entries, and removed per piece on a swap; 0x2EA18C adds a count, 0x6E90F4 subtracts and removes an entry at zero. A piece's Tint is a Model/SimpleModelTint (76 records) that maps the tint mask's R, G, B and A channels to palette slots; index 16 means unused. The writer 0x36B430 walks the visual's 23 pieces: for each piece with a Tint it finds or creates the tint entry (0x4C3634) and, per channel below 16, 0x2EAF10 - 0x2EAFF4 writes the layer: when the palette entry's alpha is 0xFF, amount 1.0 and colour (R, G, B) / 255 ( SetParamVector , handle slot 7); otherwise amount 0.0 and no colour record. On the head (slot 1) the tattoo layer is gated by SimpleModel.TattooApplyToHead and war paint by PaintApplyToHead (true on 182 of 185 SimpleModels). The eye shader tints the iris by the G layer (the eye palette entry) and writes an emissive value saturate((mask . k vEmissiveTintChannelMask - range.x) / (range.y - range.x)) x k fEmissiveScale : orc heads ship range (0, 2) and scale 0.05 (0.35 bright, 0 cataracts), so a fully masked pixel glows at half the scale; Olog heads have no eye glow. x: - Easterling armour pieces use the orc rig's bone names (the heavy chest 71 of 74 bones; only the collar bones are missing). Orc Buff FaceCape Chest and the Druid legs and pants have no second UV set in their LOD0 mesh while using a LOD0 material, so they vanish in close-up. - 69 armour pieces belong to items no shipped record references (Druid pants and legs, Underclothes, Leather shoulders, the Buff Defender set, Easterling heavy and plate pieces ...); 15 cut pieces ship no mesh in any archive (the Buff Defender set, two Celebrimbor rings, a cinematic hair ...). - Who reads a design's OutOfMemoryBackups ( AD Black Shoulders - AD Sauron Shoulders ), and when does the engine fall back to it? - How a spawned body picks up a rebuilt appearance object, and whether the engine supports a body type change on a loaded character; a live comparison of [FM+0x2D8] with the visual's +0xB8 before and after a level-up would settle the first. - How Rogue BodyTattoo (no material override, so the give path files nothing) applies the Rogue body, and which items carry the LOD painted variants. - What piece slots 6, 14 and 18-22 hold, if anything; no build step or design writes them. - How the body-animation marker items ( Personality UniqueBodyAnim IT , no payload) reach the animation, and how the ChildItemPicker tint items ( IT Faction Enemy Tint ) are resolved, since the give path reads neither.

Captains are FactionMember objects (see The Nemesis system). Their strengths, weaknesses, class bonus, advanced class, gangs and quirks are all traits, held in trait slots and resolved by the engine from data.

FactionMember offset Meaning --- --- +0x1E0 the trait slot vector {begin, end, u32 capacity at +0x10, u8 owned at +0x14} ; a slot is 0x20 bytes (below) +0x198 the active trait set, a vector of 8-byte Faction/Traits/Definitions pointers (it equals the set of slot traits in 528 of 531 captains) +0x1B0 the marker vector ( Marker records) +0x378 a cache: the first active trait with GangLeader (0x1BC3CB4) +0x508 derived bits: 14 any CanBypassRequiredDataLevelToSpawn , 19 any NPC summon / gang, 43 a trait that forbids sim events with a boss, 34 the slot list needs sorting, 38 the engine refuses trait edits (0x114B55C) A slot is +0x00 the Faction/Traits/Picker , +0x08 the trait it resolved to (null = nothing), +0x10 the trait a story mission unlocked for it, +0x18 a u16 flag word, +0x1A an i16 option index (-1 = none). A picker's options are Picker.Traits - StructuresFactionTraitPickerEntry records ( .Trait ). 493 pickers exist.

t: The flag word is the gate list and the re-roll mask
x: When a slot is added, its u16 at +0x18 is copied from the faction system's table FS+0xE0 (indexed by the picker's record index; 18,508 of 18,508 entries match). It is two things at once: - the gate list - 0x1234E0(&slot+0x18, bit) ( bt ) decides which tests the resolver runs: bit 1 minimum level, 2 required row rank, 3 player follower, 4 required other traits, 6 intel level, 7 a campaign predicate, 8 difficulty; - the re-roll mask - the resolver 0x3528C4 first ANDs the rebuild's reason mask with it and, when the result is 0, returns slot+0x08 unchanged (0x352AB8: xor eax,eax; cmp word [rcx],ax; sete al ). A slot is re-decided only by the events whose bit it carries. Every picker carries bit 0 (493 of 493), so reason 0 re-rolls every slot. No live slot has a flag word of 0 (19,713 slots), so a zero word marks a slot that the engine will never re-roll: the resolver returns its trait for every reason. The resolver returns the first option whose flagged gates all pass. Options with MissionUnlock MinXPLevel set additionally require the level to reach the remapped MissionUnlock - 1 (0x352DB8) and the option's trait to equal slot+0x10 (0x3529A3); +0x10 is 0 on every live slot. A scripted scene is a presentation. The scripts queue a relay on the player: System:GetPlayer():QueuePresentation(DBPresentationRelay.FortAssault Intro, overlord) . The native call is CPlayerObj::QueuePresentation 0x734C30(player, relay, target) - 0x734C7C(the player's scene component [player+0x2FC0] , relay, target), which builds a message holding the relay's Event , the target handle (0x18D888) and a camera type (message +0x78 ). The chain is relay - event - sequence pool - the first sequence whose predicate passes - elements. Each element sets a camera, a duration or an advance hook, script keys, voice and actions; an action is {source actor, target actor, AnimType or AudioKey} . A sequence plays only if every predicate passes; WarchiefIntro EVT , for example, tries the mounted betrayal, the betrayal, the failed spy chief and finally the default.

- The target actor ( Target ACT , Overlord ACT ) is the relay's target, tested by the AssumedTargetPredicate . - Extra actors (a failed spy chief, a betrayer, a beast) come from ExtraTargetPredicates . The binder 0x4303E4 takes the first character in a candidate list that passes its object predicate and is not already bound. 0x6FD134 picks the list: relay messages (types 14 / 15) use [base+0x27265B0] , every spawned character (it keeps corpses too: about 60 of 120 entries in a battle); other messages use [base+0x2728EE8] , a subset of about 12. - Object predicates bind actors mostly by inventory items , which the scene scripts hand out ( AddInventoryItem ). The sequence evaluator 0x3650B4 (called per pool entry by the start routine 0x43E6B8; the queued message is its context: subject at ctx+0x88 , source at ctx+0x80 ) tests, in order: the player predicate; the source predicate (a source, when present, must pass the object predicate and is bound to its actor by 0x43EE28; a failure fails the branch); the assumed-target predicate (the subject; none fails the branch); the player's-target predicate (0x182B5F0 - 0x523B0C( [player+0x2FA0] ) = the player's own combat object's current targe

The camera filter 0x4328DC compares each pool entry's CameraType and CameraVariantRequireAny with the active type [ctx+0x38] and variant [ctx+0x40] . The type is decided when the relay is queued (0x734E1C): the relay's own CameraType (at +0x20 in every relay, a link to Presentation/Predicates/Types/Camera ), otherwise, when QuestCameraType is set, the PresentationCameraType of the first running quest. Siege quests carry <Region FortAssault CT , so the fixed fortress shots exist only inside a siege. The variant (A or B, the two sides an assault can start from) comes from the sequence's CameraVariance picker. t: The scene clock and slow motion
x: Every element duration is a timer at +0x288 of the running presentation, on the clock [base+0x2702578] (0x37B784 - 0x37BCE4; expiry is bit 1 of pres+0x6C ). The engine keeps five scaled clocks, which slow motion drives as channels (0x5CF888): 0 the world [base+0x2702598] , 1 the player [base+0x2702548] , 2 the combat companion [base+0x2702570] , 3 the world UI [base+0x2702558] and 4 presentations [base+0x2702578] . 0x5CF834 writes a clock's numerator, denominator and scale at [clock+8]+0x28 / +0x2C / +0x30 ; 0x5CEBB4 resets it to 1/1. A slow-motion instance stores channel c as {+0x44 enabled, +0x48 scale} + c 0xC . Period and ramp-up timers run on [base+0x2702550] (UI: [base+0x2702588] ), which slow motion never scales. The slow-motion manager is MainScene+0x7A8 (ticked by the scene tick): requested instances at +0x00 / +0x08 , the running one at +0x38 (the update 0x5CF55C picks the lowest priority at instance+0x80 ; requests go through 0x5D08B8). An instance copies its SlowMo record's scales at Start (0x5CEC10), and the manager re-runs Start whenever its current instance changes. t: Driving a movie from code: the node API
x: The engine wraps every Scaleform value it touches in a 0xF8-byte node (vt 0x1DAB888, constructor 0x1C309C): +0x28 the value's object interface, +0x30 the value type ( (type & 0x8F) == 0xA is a display object), +0x38 the object. Callers receive nodes through output handles that the callee constructs in place (0x1C2F80, the node at handle+0x10 ); a handle holds pointers to itself, so it cannot be moved once constructed, and its destructor 0x1C68FC releases the node. Call Address Arguments --- --- --- root wrapper vf42 0x4679C4 (wrapper, out) GetVariable 0x467A20 ( [wrapper+0x18] , value, "path"): resolves root , not clips attached at run time GetMember node vf83 0x1C2EE4 (node, out, "name") GetMember by path node vf84 0x11C063C (node, out, "a.b.c") createEmptyMovieClip node vf80 0x7B1EE4 (node, out, "name"): creates the clip; returns an empty handle when the name exists attachMovie node vf76 0x474434 (node, out, "symbol", "instance"), both char ; refuses an existing instance name (0x47482C) removeMovieClip node vf86 0xEBDAC (node) Invoke without arguments node vf85 0x11C10B4 (node, "method"); the general invoke is 0x4676C0 play / stop node vf121 0xEBDE4 / vf122 0xEBE0C (node) gotoAnd

An attached clip lives exactly as long as the node attachMovie returned. attachMovie allocates the node, attaches the symbol (0x115BB34), then 0x4744EC sets the owner byte node+0x58 to 1 and registers an onUnload listener at node+0xA0 whose callback is 0x7941C4. The node destructor (vf0 0x1C3158 - 0x1C318C) releases the listener and, while +0x58 is set, invokes removeMovieClip on the clip. If the clip is unloaded some other way (removed, or its parent removed), 0x7941C4 clears +0x58 first, so a clip is never removed twice. Lookup nodes (GetMember vf83 / vf84, root ) never set the owner byte. So releasing an attach handle removes the clip, and a lookup handle for the same clip is a different node whose release leaves the clip alone. Code that keeps attached clips on screen must hold their attach handles (and release children before parents).

t: Saves, the store and the network layer

x: A Steam save is Steam\userdata\<account \356190\remote\<account hex <slot ShadowOfWar.sav ; the file-name prefix is the Steam account number in hexadecimal. header 'SOM3' u32 salt u32 padded length (= file size - 16, a multiple of 16) u32 real length body AES-256-CBC, PKCS 7 padding key 256 bits, derived per file from a constant built into the executable, the header's salt and the owning account's number (SOM2 files leave the account out) iv a constant built into the executable The reader 0x119A2C8 accepts SOM2 and SOM3 ( sub eax,'SOM2'; test eax,0xFEFFFFFF ); the writer is 0x52B4BC. Both use OpenSSL's EVP layer linked into the executable ( EVP aes 256 cbc , the decrypt init / update / final calls and the padding switch). The padding byte equals padded length minus real length, and the plaintext's entropy drops from 8.00 to 5.01 bits per byte. This reference describes the format; it does not publish the key material.

The plaintext opens with SAVE version 2: a header (a u32 profile-section count at +0x18 , 5), the profile sections, a u32 slot count (3), then per slot {u32 6, u32 length, u32 0, payload} . A section is tag, u32 version, u32 size, u32 0, u32 n (= size - 4), n bytes of typed values: Tag Value --- --- 00 a 32-bit name hash (4 bytes) 02 u8 04 u32 05 two u32 (a GUID half, a pair of counters) 08 i32 0A f32 0C bool (1 byte) 0E vec3 (12 bytes; positions in cm) 0F byte string (u8 length + bytes: GUID text, a product id) 10 u32, the byte size of what follows With these ten tags, 27 of 27 sections of a story slot read to their exact end. GameDB records are saved as name hashes, never as strings (a 2.3 MB save holds 421 ASCII tokens, all settings); the hash does not carry a category, so the section's context decides which category it names. Layout. 86 sections: 5 profile sections ( GOXC PERF PICB GPDC GMSC ) and the same 27 in each of the 3 slots. Per slot, in file order: SAVE (the summary, version 31), a u32 giving the byte length of the rest of the slot, IVGD (v3), ENT2 IVSH PPDC PDIC PAIC IEUC IVMG (v43), IVPD (v4), TTRL LTMR , about 1.28 MB with no typed section header, then FAST FOTP ASM

Shadow of Mordor (2014) is the predecessor engine generation. Its internal project name is Firebird ; Shadow of War's is Kraken . The two games share their archive family, container idea, GameDB format and much of their orc rig, but nearly every asset format moved on by several versions, so no Mordor asset loads in War unchanged.

Shadow of Mordor Shadow of War --- --- --- x64 executable ShadowOfMordor.exe , 27,930,624 bytes ShadowOfWar.exe , 117,732,784 bytes Load address 0x140000000 preferred, relocatable ( DYNAMIC BASE , relocation table present) always 0x140000000 (relocations stripped) Code a conventional .text section of about 20.6 MB .arch (about 30 MB) plus 70 MB of code in .bss a (see The executable) Because Mordor's executable is relocatable, its addresses move with ASLR every run; War's static addresses never move.

Both games use LTAR archives. Mordor's are version 3 ( .arch05 ), War's version 4 ( .arch06 , see Archives and file formats). The Mordor install has 66 archives, 45.4 GB . header (0x18 bytes) "LTAR" u32 version (3) u32 names size u32 folder count u32 file count u32 1 names null-separated strings from 0x18; the last string may run past the declared size, and a small block precedes the entry table entry (0x20 bytes) u64 data offset u64 compressed size u64 uncompressed size u32 flag (9) u32 name offset The entry table is found by its signature (the flag 9 at +0x18 of consecutive entries). Parsing all 66 archives gives 28,884 entries, equal to the 28,884 declared in the headers ; every entry's data lies inside its file and the data offsets ascend in all 28,828 consecutive pairs. A name offset may point into the middle of a string, and an entry's name does not reliably describe its payload, so asset paths are taken from the containers' own path tables, as in War. Compression. Mordor stores each entry as a stream of chunks {u32 compressed length, u32 uncompressed length (at most 65,536), data} compressed with zlib ; chunks whose two lengths are equal are stored uncompressed (of 192 sampl

Mordor's containers are BNDL version 4 (War: version 6); 8,034 of them hold 67,982 asset paths (66,731 distinct). Mordor's world prefabs are PRFB version 5 and its Scaleform movies GFX version 8 (ActionScript 2). Asset formats are older versions that War's loaders reject: Format Shadow of Mordor Shadow of War --- --- --- mesh ( MMSH ) 9 16-17 skeleton ( SKEL ) 8 (War's loader rejects it) texture ( TEXR ) 3 8 material instance ( LTMI ) 4 7-8 Mordor's version-9 mesh vertex is 60 bytes: half-precision position (4 halves), 16-bit texture coordinates, 32-bit normal, tangent and bitangent, a colour, blend weights in BGRA order and bone indices; strides can differ between a mesh's elements. Every Mordor mesh has one UV set , while War's orc gear shaders read a second one. Mordor's texture coordinates can run to 2.0. Textures use the same DDS-based payload, and War's texture header adds a 23-byte block. Materials are authored differently: Mordor's orcs use about 21 generic shaders, War's use the dedicated nemesis gear, head and body shader trees (see Rendering). For the one weapon compared directly (the Master Pike), Mordor's albedo was about half as bright as War's equivalent (mean 56 / 4

Mordor's GameDB is a GADB version 17 file (the same container version as War's; see GameDB) of 23,264,671 bytes inside hotchunk.arch05 's globaldatabase bundle: the entry after the named manifest entry, a BNDL v4 wrapping the database. It holds 115 character models named Cha . The Black Númenórean characters are three unique models: Cha Belroth (the Hammer), Cha Imrakhad (the Tower) and Cha Zainzadan (the Black Hand, whose mesh one of Talion's alternative skins in Mordor is built from). Mordor ships no generic Black Númenórean soldier armour: a census of every container path (66,731 distinct), every self-named texture (12,714, none unreferenced) and every XML manifest (8,071) finds none. The warband downloads ( layer52 to layer56 archives) are 216-byte unlock stubs: the Guardian, Blood Hunter, Crusher and Flesh Burner orcs are GameDB presets assembling base-game pieces with paint, not new assets.

Mordor's hierarchy screen is a world of its own, worlds\cinematics\wraith visions\hierarchymenu son.bndl ( son.arch05 entry 15, 232,667,989 bytes, 446 assets; near-identical copies in intro.arch05 and outro.arch05 ): a scene, an object database, a world mesh and 10 prefabs (the hierarchy art, the Warchief pedestals, glyphs, orc light posts, a ruin wall, backdrop rocks), with the crowd drawn as card meshes ( fx\ui\hierarchy\models\orcarmy outlinecards.mesh ). The seats are logical rows and columns in StructuresFaction.HierarchyFactionPos (5 Warchiefs and captain rows of 8, 7 and 5: 25 seats), placed in the world as objects Hier.Faction <row <column with a character spot .Chr , a camera .Cam and about 20 points of interest each. The screen's movie is interface\flash\widgets\hierarchy.gfx , which holds no logic.

t: The Mordor importer in Shadow of War
x: Shadow of War ships an importer that rebuilds a player's Shadow of Mordor nemesis as a War captain or follower, compiled from ...\KRAKEN CODE STREAM\source\Game\Shared\NemesisForgeUtils.cpp (log tag [NEMESISFORGE]: ; the logger is compiled out of the shipping build). The check. The loading-progress tick 0x1E3E78 ( [GM+0x6D30] ) calls 0x1B3ABFC. It returns without checking when either of two state bytes of its object ( +0x38 , +0x80 ) is set, or when the predicate Invasion/Settings.HaltNemesisForgeCheckPredicate (the settings record at +0x468 ) evaluates true. Otherwise it tail-jumps to 0x1B3AA94, which builds an online request carrying the player's FirebirdProfileID and platform and registers 0x1B32CD0 as its completion handler. The data therefore comes from the publisher's online service, not from Mordor's local save. The conversion. When an army's pool is filled (0xFD51A0, the Faction/Definition.Pool consumer) an imported nemesis goes through 0x1BC05D0, which logs its name and faction and calls 0x1C6369C.
